sweep_summary: One item in this search of works with stress in the title: Walker 2002 (NELS 32), already listed in the per-language bibliography. Previous check could not obtain it (scholarworks 403; the USC asset URL cited by Semantic Scholar is dead). Located the author's copy on Rachel Walker's UCSC site (publications page) and downloaded it with wget (automated download was refused by the CampusPress host). The paper is about augmentation in the locative/future suffixes; its only stress statement (p. 552) is background taken from Lopes & Parker 1999: 332: main stress on the last stem syllable, suffixes generally excluded from the stem domain, stressed vowels lengthen, every morpheme contributing exactly one syllable. This CONFIRMS the catalog's set by morphology coding based on Lopes 1995 (stem-final primary stress, suffixes extrametrical) and does not supersede it (second-hand; silent on the plural-suffix exception and secondary stress). Not in the item list but flagged from Walker's citations: Lopes & Parker 1999, 'Aspects of Yuhup Phonology', IJAL 65(3): 324-342 (doi 10.1086/466393, paywalled per our earlier reading), p. 332 is the pinpointed published first-hand stress statement and would be the best acquisition target (high priority) if a copy becomes available. all look-ups were done through APIs (Semantic Scholar, Glottolog) and direct downloads.

This is a second-hand statement (explicitly drawn from Lopes & Parker 1999: 332, the published IJAL version of the catalog's source Lopes 1995), so it is an independent published restatement rather than new first-hand data. new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog's stem-final stress statement and silent on placement; adds that high tone is the phonetic correlate of the stressed syllable and that the language also has contrastive contour tones (so 'stress' and 'tone' coexist). The quote is Díaz's Spanish summary of Martins 2005, not first-hand data. new_statements.rule_in_words: Yuhup has lexical (contrastive) rising and falling tones; the phonetic high vs. low register tones are correlates of word stress (high on the stressed syllable, low on unstressed ones). The work says nothing about where in the word the stressed syllable falls; the only stress sentence is this second-hand summary of Martins 2005: 94-97 in a comparison table, and the thesis is otherwise about nasality (instrumental phonetics).
new_statements.identity_note: Díaz 2009 is a Bogotá (Universidad Nacional de Colombia) thesis on the Colombian Yuhup of the Vaupés, drawing on Ospina Bozzi's Colombian data; Martins 2005 and Lopes & Parker 1999 describe Brazilian Yuhup (Rio Tiquié area). Moore 1977 concerns Hupda, not Yuhup.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is predictable (non-contrastive). Primary stress falls on the final syllable of the word computed with affixes extrametrical, i.e. on the last syllable of the stem (with mostly monosyllabic morphemes, the last root); prefixes and suffixes are unstressed, except that the plural suffix is metrical and takes the final primary stress; when two suffixes follow the stem both are extrametrical. Formalised as right-headed binary (iambic) feet built right-to-left with a right-headed unbounded word constituent (Halle & Vergnaud 1987). The stressed vowel is lengthened (duration is the phonetic correlate; monosyllables have long vowels, tone-bearing words extra-long vowels). Tone: rising vs falling contour contrastive only in nine noun/adjective minimal pairs; elsewhere non-contrastive, interpreted as vestiges of an earlier tonal system.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Secondary stress on the first syllable of the word (in words of three or more syllables, e.g. [,poregõ'ho:h] 'avião', and on a prefix or first stem syllable before a stressed plural suffix, e.g. [,tih-wah-'dəh] 'os antigos').
new_statements.exceptions: Plural suffix is not extrametrical (it receives the final primary stress); words with two suffixes: both extrametrical, stress on the stem ([,kə:'ro?-ih-mõh] 'respondeu'); Portuguese loanwords keep penultimate stress ([pa'pera], [ku'jera], [mu'turu], p. 16); in reduplicated words and complex nuclei the first vowel is short and the second carries length and stress (pp. 21, 53).
new_statements.identity_note: Lopes 1995 describes Yuhup (Makú/Naduhup) as spoken by c. 400 people in ten communities on the Tiquié, Apaporis and Traíra rivers (Brazil/Colombia border, upper Rio Negro); data from seven named speakers collected from August 1986 and revised January-October 1994 (SIL fieldwork, CECIL 1.2 measurements); no dialect is distinguished. Díaz 2009's tone statement concerns the Colombian variety (Ospina's 2008 data).

tone_statements.quote: Fundamentado na análise do acento e na inter-relação entre tom e acento, propõe-se que em Yuhup há palavras tonais e palavras atonais. As palavras com tons podem conter os tons ascendente / / e descendente / /. As palavras atonais têm dois tons fonéticos produzidos pelo sistema acentual, um tom baixo [ ] , que ocorre na sílaba não-acentuada e, um tom alto [ ] , atribuído à sílaba acentuada (cf. 2.3.4). (...) As palavras que possuem tom baixo e/ou alto são interpretadas fonologicamente como atonais, pois não há contraste tonal entre esses dois tons, posto que estes tons são previsíveis. (...) Em Yuhup, há palavras que se opõem exclusivamente pelos tons. [tone diacritics inside / / and [ ] are lost in the PDF text layer]
tone_statements.translation: Based on the analysis of accent and the interrelation between tone and accent, it is proposed that Yuhup has tonal words and atonal words. Words with tones may carry the rising / / and falling / / tones. Atonal words have two phonetic tones produced by the accentual system, a low tone [ ], which occurs on the unstressed syllable, and a high tone [ ], assigned to the stressed syllable (cf. 2.3.4). (...) Words that have low and/or high tone are interpreted phonologically as atonal, since there is no tonal contrast between these two tones, given that these tones are predictable. (...) In Yuhup there are words that contrast exclusively by their tones.
tone_statements.locator: Ch. II sec. 2.3.5 'Tom', pp. 94-95; one-line summary also at sec. 2.3 intro, p. 79
tone_statements.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)
tone_statements.summary: Fixed word-final accent with predictable phonetic H (stressed) / L (unstressed); two contrastive lexical contour tones, rising and falling, on tonal (monosyllabic) words, also used derivationally (deverbal nouns) and for the imperative; no coda-voicing restriction (unlike Hup); tones derived historically from a Proto-Eastern-Maku accentual/length system.

tone_statements.citation: Epps, Patience. 2005. A grammar of Hup. PhD dissertation, University of Virginia.
tone_statements.quote: The most striking aspect of Hup's tone system from a comparative perspective is its nearly mirror-image resemblance to the tone (word-accent) system in Yuhup. While the word-final lexical stress pattern is essentially the same in the two languages, rising tone on Yuhup words corresponds quite consistently to high (falling) tone on their Hup cognates; likewise, high/falling tone in Yuhup corresponds to rising tone in Hup. The same allophony between falling tone and high tone (dependent on whether the coda consonant is voiced or voiceless, respectively) exists in both languages.

readall_conflicts: No disagreement on stress placement: Lopes 1995 (thesis, = catalog source), Walker 2002 citing Lopes & Parker 1999: 332, and Martins 2005 (via Díaz 2009 and the folder's earlier check) all put primary stress on the last syllable of the word/stem with ordinary suffixes outside the stress domain; Lopes 1995 adds initial secondary stress and the plural-suffix exception, on which the others are silent. The only divergence is about tone, not stress: Lopes 1995 finds contour tone contrastive in just nine minimal pairs and otherwise non-contrastive (a tonal residue), whereas Díaz 2009 (summarising Martins 2005: 94-97 and Ospina 2002) describes two phonologically distinctive contour tones with high/low register tracking stressed/unstressed syllables. The cited IJAL article (Lopes & Parker 1999) itself remains unread, so its own wording on stress and tone could not be checked.

sources.note: First-hand grammar sketch ('Esta breve descrição gramatical é baseada em análise própria', p. 78; the authors have worked with the Tiquié Yuhupdeh since 2006). States that stress is predictable and always on the last syllable, and that the contour tones which accompany the accent fall on the last syllable of morphological roots: the same rule as the catalog's coding from Lopes 1995 (root/stem-final primary stress). Silent on secondary stress and on the plural-suffix exception. The row also remains the source of the record's morphology census.

tone.translation: Based on the analysis of accent and the interrelation between tone and accent, it is proposed that Yuhup has tonal words and atonal words. Words with tones may carry the rising / / and falling / / tones. Atonal words have two phonetic tones produced by the accentual system, a low tone [ ], which occurs on the unstressed syllable, and a high tone [ ], assigned to the stressed syllable (cf. 2.3.4). (...) Words that have low and/or high tone are interpreted phonologically as atonal, since there is no tonal contrast between these two tones, given that these tones are predictable. (...) In Yuhup there are words that contrast exclusively by their tones.
tone.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)
tone.summary: Fixed word-final accent with predictable phonetic H (stressed) / L (unstressed); two contrastive lexical contour tones, rising and falling, on tonal (monosyllabic) words, also used derivationally (deverbal nouns) and for the imperative; no coda-voicing restriction (unlike Hup); tones derived historically from a Proto-Eastern-Maku accentual/length system.

sources.note: A case study of tonogenesis in Naduhup; proposes that Naduhup tone arose from a prior vowel-length contrast linked to coda voicing, with contact with neighbouring tonal (Tukanoan) languages as a catalyst; shows how vowel length, coda voicing and intonation feed the emergence of tone. Contents on Yuhup specifically (tone contours figure) unseen.
